newsitem.title: UK: Study links asthma with thunderstorms.
newsitem.headline: Study links asthma with thunderstorms.

text.p: British doctors said on Wednesday heavy thunderstorms can cause outbreaks of asthma.
They said a severe thunderstorm that hit the southeast of England in 1994 caused a fourfold increase in the number of asthma attacks.

Katherine Venables of the National Heart Institute in London and Jonathan Higham of Cambridge University's Institute of Public Health analysed records for emergency calls made during the thunderstorm and compared them to records for a night the week before.
"It was a very sizeable epidemic of asthma. There is no question about that," Venables said in a telephone interview.
She said the thunderstorm could have had an effect on grass pollen. An as-yet unpublished study shows most of the victims were known to react to grass.
"It happened just after the main peak of grass pollen in the southeast," said Venables, who reported the findings in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.
Thunderstorms are known to break up pollen grains into smaller pieces. Finer pollen particles would cause a bigger asthmatic reaction.
"We think it effectively delivered a high dose of pollen to pollen-sensitive people," she said.
Temperature and humidity swings could also be responsible, or the effect of the electricity from lightning on pollen particles.
